title: Kurma
tomorrow: a cow, a horse, a goddess rise from the sea. real, or a picture?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kurma: the tortoise under the sinking mountain, holding from below so the churning could go on. They churn for nectar. So why does poison come up first?

Look closely at a picture of Shiva and there's a strange detail at his throat: it's blue. Not his face, his throat. The answer is in the churning. The gods and asuras are pulling, the tortoise is holding, the sea is foaming, and the first thing to rise out of the ocean of milk isn't nectar. It's halahala, a poison so fierce the world starts to burn.
screen: `A BLUE THROAT. WHY?` → `THE SEA IS FOAMING.` → `HALAHALA RISES FIRST.`

segments.voice: No one planned for this. They came for amrita, and the sea gave them poison first. The gods and asuras can't handle it, and they don't pretend they can. They go to Shiva and ask for help. In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, Shiva takes the poison in his hand and drinks it, out of compassion for everyone suffering. It doesn't kill him. It stays in his throat and turns it dark blue, and so one of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated one. In some tellings, Parvati presses his throat so the poison goes no further. So the puzzle is solved: the blue is the mark of something taken in so others wouldn't burn. And look where the tortoise is during all this: still underneath. The churning turned up something terrible, and it didn't stop, because the mountain still had its footing. One holds the work from below. One takes in what's too harsh for anyone else. Between them, the churning can go on toward what it was for. The story keeps that order, poison first and treasures after, and it doesn't pretend a long, hard work only brings up good things.
screen: `POISON FIRST, NOT NECTAR.` · `THE GODS ASK SHIVA FOR HELP.` · `NILAKANTHA: THE BLUE THROAT.` · then, large: `THE WORK STILL HOLDS.`

segments.voice: With a pen and any scrap of paper, write one hard thing that's come up lately, in a few plain words. Under it, write one thing that's still holding: a person, a habit, a place to stand. Fold it, and breathe slowly for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can hold both before God.
Kurma: the tortoise who keeps holding, even when the churning brings up poison first.
The line to take with you: Kurma, where the poison comes up first and the work still holds. See you tomorrow.
